article.title: Controlling Unalienable Rights
article.author: Chuck Yates
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Early voting opened here in Idaho on October 19, and we were among the first to go in and exercise our franchise. The ballot this time includes four measures for voters to consider. One is an invitation to designate the official state gun. Choices include one modern rifle, two World War II icons, and three Wild West classics. In a state where six of every ten people own guns, this measure is not surprising. The others are less frivolous. Two of them would amend the state constitution in consequential ways. House Joint Resolution 4 would grant the legislature sole authority to legalize marijuana and other psychoactive substances, depriving voters of any further say in the matter. House Joint Resolution 6 would make English the official language of the state, requiring all official and public business to be conducted in only in that language. The fourth measure, Proposition 1, “The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act,” would alleviate some of the state’s restrictions on abortion. As set forth in the current law, Title 18-622, “The Defense of Life Act,” abortion is legal in Idaho only in cases of medical emergency, rape, or incest. A physician may act to save the life of the mother, but survivors of rape or incest must report incidents and provide official documentation within the first thirteen weeks. Related: The National Anthem and America's Dangerous Brand of Patriotism Title 18-622 complicates the lives of those in need of an abortion, but it’s not aimed at them. It’s aimed at everyone involved in performing abortions. The law classifies abortion as a felony, and those convicted of performing it or assisting in its performance would spend two to five years in prison, and could lose their licenses to practice medicine in Idaho. Thus it’s no surprise that over a third of the state’s ob/gyn specialists have either left or stopped practicing. Ostensibly, the intent of 18-622 is to defend the life of the fetus in the womb. But it does not defend the life of a fetus in the womb of a woman whose own life is endangered, or in the womb of a survivor of rape or incest. Depending on circumstances, then, the lives of some fetuses are just not worthy of defense. In other words, the “defense of life” ordained by 18-622 is not “pro-life.” In some cases, as specified in the statute, it’s actually anti-life. Proposition 1 would create a new chapter in the Idaho statutes, not in Title 18, “Crimes and Punishments,” but in Title 39, “Health and Safety.” It would establish a right “to make private reproductive health care decisions, including abortion up to fetal viability and in medical emergencies....Notwithstanding any other provision of law to the contrary....”—that is, regardless of anything in 18-622. The new law, Title 39-8, would retain the restrictions imposed by 18-622, limiting abortion to the first trimester, with exceptions only to save the mother’s life or in cases of rape or incest. But it would decriminalize the performance of abortions, and it would remove the threat of imprisonment and loss of professional credentials for those performing them. And it would restore individual agency. Note well: the restrictions on abortion itself would not change, only the state-imposed social control. Related: Major Jason Watson, Trump, and the Military’s Duty to Defy Illegal Orders Specifically, Title 39-8 “recognizes that reproductive health care choices...are deeply private matters,” and it “upholds a person’s rights to make their own decisions based on their own values, health care needs, and circumstances—free from the fear of external pressures or punitive consequences....” The choice would be that of the pregnant woman and no one else. No parent, guardian, public official, or sexual partner would have any role in the matter, unless invited to participate. Opponents of Proposition 1 claim that it would establish “abortion on demand,” and turn abortion into an unregulated free for all. More likely, what they object to is the assumption behind its key terms, “personal” and “private.” It would eliminate the right of the state, and of individuals, to interfere in a process that properly involves only the person going through it and those assisting her. In other words, the controversy likely isn’t as much about abortion as it is about who gets to decide, and who doesn’t. Opponents of abortion have their reasons, and certainly no one actually approves of or desires abortion, except as a justified last resort. For some, abortion is an atrocity, not different from the Final Solution except in magnitude. For others, it’s more analogous to an amputation, deeply tragic but in some cases necessary. In the end, what it comes down to is that a patriarchal surveillance state cannot permit its subjects to enjoy liberties such as those specified in Proposition 1. The existing law effectively deprives everyone in Idaho of exactly those liberties defined elsewhere as “unalienable rights” to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” The chief purpose of Proposition 1 is to restore those rights.
